newsitem.title: SPAIN: Politicians back weaker peseta, currency falls.
newsitem.headline: Politicians back weaker peseta, currency falls.

text.p: The gradual weakening of the peseta this week has coincided with declarations by senior politicians indicating they consider the exchange rate of the Spanish currency is too high.
"I would like it if (the peseta) was not so strong, but the market rules," Budget Secretary Jose Folgado told Reuters in an interview on Monday.
At 1600 GMT on Wednesday, the peseta was trading at 84.57/59 to the mark, against 84.12/14 in early trade Monday and levels of around 83 to the mark last week.
Folgado's comments echoed those of Joaquin Molins, parliamentary spokesman for the government's Catalan allies, Convergence and Unity (CiU).

There is a consensus in the market that the ideal exchange rate for the peseta to go into the first phase of Europe's planned single currency is around its Exchange Rate Mechanism central parity rate of 85.0718 pesetas per mark.
But it was a statement by Germany's State Secretary at the Finance Ministry Juergen Stark that sent the peseta and other peripheral European currencies sliding versus the German currency.

In comments thought to be aimed at the peripheral European countries, Stark said that some countries which qualify on paper for European economic and monetary union (EMU) would be advised to stay on the sidelines until their stability was proven.
"Stark's comments have contributed to the general strengthening of the mark," Banco Bilbao Vizcaya's (BBV) strategy director Antonio Pulido said.

But analysts did not expect the peseta to move much further from its present rate versus the mark. "I don't think the depreciation will go much further than 84.60 (pesetas per mark)", said Carmen Hernansanz, economist at Merrill Lynch Espana.
Some saw it at around 85 per mark.
"The 85 level could provide firm support for the peseta whilst the Bank of Spain could hold it up with its strong reserves," BBV's Pulido said.
Domestic economic fundamentals were healthy enough to hold up the currency at present levels, analysts said.
A strong dollar also provided good support for the peseta.
"While the dollar remains strong, the depreciation of the peseta will be limited," said one analyst.
But analysts also said that all the good news was already factored into market prices and thus anything which questions Spain's inclusion in EMU could upset the markets.
"The market has discounted a lot, and consequently the situation now is more delicate," said Pulido.
